title: AI just went multiplayer. Your engineering metrics have to count every player.
summary: Waydev - AI just went multiplayer. Your engineering metrics have to count every player.
body_markdown:
Agentic engineering


AI just went multiplayer. Your engineering metrics have to count every player.


Atlassian wants AI agents to stop working in private chat windows and start working as visible, accountable members of the team. That is the right move. It also raises the question every engineering leader will be asked next: now that we can see what agents did, was it worth it?


AC


**Alex Circei** CEO and Co-Founder, Waydev


At Team ’26 Europe in Amsterdam on October 7, Atlassian announced the[Agentic Multiplayer Protocol (AMP)](https://www.atlassian.com/platform/agentic-multiplayer-protocol) . The idea is simple to state and hard to build: AI agents should take part in shared work the way people do, inside the same governed system, rather than as tools each person consults alone.


AMP is grounded in Atlassian’s Teamwork Graph, which the company says now links more than 250 billion objects and relationships across work items, documents, people and code. Around it, Atlassian shipped a rebuilt MCP server with more than 200 tools (already handling around 15 million tool calls a day), Rovo Work for multi-step tasks that humans review and approve, and code indexing down to functions, symbols and classes across Bitbucket and GitHub, with GitLab support announced as coming.


## What AMP gives an agent


Strip away the product names and AMP defines five things every agent needs to be a real participant in team work.


1


**Identity** A distinct profile and a named human owner, so “who did this?” always has an answer.


2


**Permissions** Scoped authority over what the agent may read and change, governed centrally.


3


**Shared context** The same organizational knowledge the humans on the team work from.


4


**Concrete tasks** Work assigned in the open, through Jira, Confluence or an @mention, not hidden in a side session.


5


**Reviewable results** Output that people can evaluate, backed by an audit trail of what the agent actually did.


A “diplomatic protocol”


That is how Atlassian CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes framed AMP: less a technical standard, more a set of rules for how humans and agents treat each other at work.


The problem


## Why engineering needed this first


Engineering is where single-player AI broke down first. A developer accepts a Copilot suggestion, pastes something from ChatGPT, hands a task to Claude Code, and lets an autonomous agent open a pull request, all in the same afternoon. Most of that happens in private sessions. When the code lands, nobody can say with confidence which parts came from a person, which came from an agent, and what context either of them had.


Multiply that across a team running several coding agents from different vendors in parallel, and you get agent sprawl: lots of output, no shared record of who or what did the work, on whose authority. Atlassian’s own leadership has said this lack of visibility into code origin is holding enterprises back from adopting AI further.


The gap


## Attribution is step one. Leaders get asked about step three.


AMP is mostly about the first two rungs of a ladder every engineering organization has to climb. The third rung is the one the CFO and the board care about.


Analysts covering the launch made the same point from a different angle. Coverage in InfoWorld noted that attribution often lives in commit messages, which developers can edit, disable or lose when history is rewritten, and that most real code is a blend of human and agent work. Attribution is easy at the edges and hard in the middle, which is exactly where most of the work now happens.


Reliable attribution lets CIOs “finally measure agentic development rather than merely count AI licenses and token consumption.”


Mike Wilkes, enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, quoted in InfoWorld


That is the real prize. Counting seats and tokens tells you what you spent. Measuring agentic development tells you what you got.


What to measure


## Multiplayer metrics for human-agent teams


Once agents have identities and owners, you can finally measure them like teammates. These are the signals we recommend engineering leaders build around.


**Contribution by owner** Agent work rolled up to the human who owns each agent, so output, quality and cost sit with someone accountable.


**Human review of agent work** How much agent output gets meaningful review, by whom, and how long approval takes as agent volume grows.


**Outcomes by origin** Change failure rate, rollbacks and rework for agent, human and blended changes, side by side.


**Handoff time** How long work waits when it passes from agent to human and back. In multiplayer work, the queue moves to the handoffs.


**Cost per outcome, per agent** As AI pricing moves to consumption, tie each agent’s spend to work that reached production, not to calls made.


**Cross-tool coverage** Which agents, repos and tools your measurement actually sees. A metric that misses half your agents is worse than no metric.


The reality


## No single graph sees the whole team


AMP is strongest where Atlassian already lives: Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, and the Teamwork Graph behind them. That is a big footprint. But very few engineering organizations run on one vendor. Code sits in GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps. Planning lives in Jira, Linear or both. Agents come from Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub, Cursor and Atlassian, often in the same team.


That is why the measurement layer has to be neutral. Identity and governance can live inside each platform. The question of whether your AI investment is paying off has to be answered across all of them, with the same definitions, for every team.


Giving agents a name tag is how you see them. Measuring their outcomes is how you decide whether to keep them.


Alex Circei, CEO, Waydev


**Where Waydev fits** Waydev is the engineering intelligence layer across your whole toolchain. It connects Git, ticketing and CI/CD data from every vendor you use, separates human and AI contribution, and measures AI adoption, impact and ROI with consistent definitions, so the multiplayer team shows up as one picture.


## The next question after “who did it?”


AMP is a meaningful step. When one of the largest collaboration platforms in software says agents need identities, owners, permissions and audit trails, the debate about whether agents are teammates is over. They are.


The harder conversation starts now. Once you can see every player, you will be asked how each one is performing, what they cost, and whether the team as a whole ships better software than it did a year ago. Engineering leaders who can answer that with data will set the pace for everyone else.
